title: How Airlines Really Make Money (It's Not Flying)
sources: IATA (Dec 2025): global airline net profit margin 3.9%, net profit per passenger ≈ $7.90 (2025–2026)
Delta Air Lines Q4/FY2025 results: American Express remuneration $8.2 billion in 2025 (+11%), expected to reach $10 billion
United Airlines 8-K (June 2020): MileagePlus appraised at $21.9 billion, used as collateral for a $5 billion financing; 2019 miles sales ≈ $5.3 billion
Bureau of Transportation Statistics: U.S. airlines collected ≈ $7.27 billion in checked bag fees in 2024
Warren Buffett, 2007 Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter (airlines as 'the worst sort of business'; Kitty Hawk joke)
U.S. airline Chapter 11 filings: United (2002), Delta (2005), American (2011)
Federal Reserve G.19: credit card accounts assessed interest ≈ 22% (2026)

beats.text: Dave just bought a plane ticket. Three hundred dollars.
A giant metal tube. Two pilots. Tons of fuel. Flying him across the country in five hours.
Guess how much profit the airline makes from Dave? About eight dollars. Less than a sandwich at the airport.
But look at this. Last year, one airline, Delta, got more than eight billion dollars from something that has nothing to do with flying.
A credit card.
Today: where your ticket money really goes, the secret money printer inside every airline, and why your airline is secretly a bank with wings.
Let's follow Dave's three hundred dollars.
A big slice goes to fuel. Jet fuel is one of the biggest costs an airline has.
Another big slice pays people. Pilots, flight attendants, mechanics, the people who load your bags.
Then the plane itself. A new passenger jet can cost more than one hundred million dollars. Airlines have to buy or rent hundreds of them.
Then airport fees, taxes, maintenance, insurance, and the tiny bag of pretzels.
When all the slices are gone, what's left for the airline? Around eight dollars out of Dave's three hundred. That's less than three cents for every dollar.
Eight dollars. For all that work. So is flying people around a good business?
Warren Buffett, one of the most famous investors in the world, once called airlines the worst sort of business.
He even joked that if a smart investor had been there when the Wright brothers took off, he should have shot the plane down. To save everyone a lot of money.
Harsh. But look at the history. United went bankrupt in two thousand two. Delta in two thousand five. American in two thousand eleven.
Why is it so hard? Because airlines fight on price. Dave searches for the cheapest ticket, and he switches airlines for ten dollars.
And one bad thing, like a fuel spike or a pandemic, can wipe out years of tiny profits.
So how do the big airlines survive? They found a much better business. Hidden in your wallet.
Remember the duck from our banking video? The money banks create out of nothing? Airlines have their own version.
It's called miles. Or points.
Here's the trick. A mile costs the airline almost nothing to create. They just type a number into Dave's account. Click. New miles.
But they don't give most miles away. They sell them. To banks.
When Dave gets an airline credit card, every time he buys a coffee, the bank gives Dave miles. And the bank has to buy those miles from the airline. With real money.
Remember the raccoon's swipe fee? The bank collects that fee from the coffee shop, and uses part of it to buy miles from the airline.
So the airline gets paid when Dave buys coffee. When Dave buys groceries. When Dave pays his phone bill. He doesn't even have to fly.
The airline prints miles like a duck lays eggs. And the bank pays cash for every egg.
How big is this? Let's look at the real numbers.
Delta has a deal with American Express. In twenty twenty five, American Express paid Delta about eight point two billion dollars. In one year.
And Delta says it expects that to grow to ten billion dollars.
Now the craziest part. In twenty twenty, the pandemic hit. Planes sat parked in the desert. Almost nobody was flying.
United Airlines needed cash, fast. So it went to the lenders and said: we'll borrow five billion dollars, and we'll use our miles program as the guarantee.
Experts valued United's miles program at about twenty two billion dollars.
At that moment, the stock market valued the entire airline, planes, airports, everything, at roughly half of that.
Read that again. The miles were worth more than the airline. The flying part was almost a bonus.
Now here's what the airline doesn't advertise. Who decides what a mile is worth?
The airline. Only the airline.
Last year, a flight to Hawaii cost Dave forty thousand miles. This year, the same seat costs sixty thousand miles.
Nobody asked Dave. His miles just bought less. That's inflation, like in our inflation video. But this time, one company controls the printer and the prices.
The airline is basically its own central bank. It prints the money, sets the prices, and can change the rules whenever it wants.
And some miles simply expire. Or get forgotten in an old account. Every forgotten mile is money the bank already paid, for a seat the airline never has to give.
The second hidden business: fees.
Airlines learned to split the ticket into pieces. The seat. The bag. Picking your seat. Boarding early. Extra legroom. A snack.
Each piece is small. But in twenty twenty four, U S airlines collected about seven point three billion dollars just from checked bags.
That's why the cheapest ticket looks so cheap. It's the bare minimum. Like a burger with no bun, no cheese, and no napkin.
Dave clicks the fifty nine dollar ticket. Then adds a bag. Then a seat next to his friend. Suddenly it's one hundred and forty dollars.
Cheap price to catch you in the search results. Fees to actually make money.
One more secret. Dave sits down, and chats with the woman next to him. Same flight. Same seat. Same pretzels.
She paid one hundred and twenty dollars. Dave paid three hundred.
How? Airlines change prices all the time. A computer watches how many seats are left, how many days until the flight, and how many people are searching.
Early on, a few seats are sold cheap, to fill the plane. As the plane fills up, the price climbs. The last seats are the most expensive.
It's like a bakery that raises the price of bread every time someone buys a loaf. The last loaf costs a fortune.
And business travelers who book last minute, because their boss told them to, often pay the most of all. Those few passengers can make the whole flight profitable.
So on the same plane, dozens of people paid dozens of different prices. Dave just booked at the wrong moment.
So should Dave stop collecting miles? Not necessarily. Here are a few simple habits people use. Education, not advice.
One. Never pay interest to earn miles. A credit card can charge around twenty two percent a year. That eats every free flight, and then some.
Two. Don't hoard. Miles tend to lose value over time. Earn them, then use them.
Three. Compare. Before using miles, check the cash price. Sometimes paying cash and saving the miles is the better deal.
And four. Look at the total price, with bags and seats, before you pick the cheapest ticket.
So let's recap.
One. Flying people barely makes money. About eight dollars a passenger.
Two. The real money printer is miles. Airlines create them for almost nothing and sell them to banks for billions.
Three. Fees and shrinking miles quietly move money from you to them.
So the next time you board a plane, remember: you're not just a passenger. You're a customer of a bank that happens to own some planes.

Subscribe, so Dave can keep explaining money. And so the raccoon doesn't steal your miles.
